title: Preposizioni Articolate
subtitle: When a, di, da, in and su fuse with the definite article.
objectives: Combine a, di, da, in and su with the definite article
Recall the fused forms al, del, dal, nel, sul and their variants
Choose the correct fused form based on the noun's article

content.intro: Five of Italian's simple prepositions fuse with a following definite article into a single word — a pattern you'll use constantly once you start referring to specific, known things.
content.explanation: Con and per also historically fuse (col, pel) but this is rare and old-fashioned in modern Italian — stick to con il/con i etc. The five that matter are a, di, da, in, su. Each combines with il/lo/la/l'/i/gli/le the same way, replacing the article's initial vowel or consonant pattern.

rules.heading: a) When to fuse
rules.body: Fuse the preposition whenever the noun that follows would itself take a definite article: Vado al cinema. (al = a + il, because "il cinema" needs il). No article, no fusion: Vado a scuola. (school with no article, a fixed expression).

rules.heading: b) Di as possession vs. dei/delle as "some"
rules.body: Del/dello/della/dei/degli/delle can also mean "some" (the partitive article, full detail at B1): Vorrei del pane. (I'd like some bread.)

examples.en: The book is on the table.
We're going to the seaside this weekend.
The key is in the bag.

examples.it: Parlo spesso degli amici che vivono all'estero.
examples.en: I often talk about the friends who live abroad.

examples.it: Il treno arriva dalla stazione centrale.
examples.en: The train arrives from the central station.

commonMistakes.why: A + il must fuse into al — they're never written as two separate words.

commonMistakes.wrong: Il libro è su il tavolo.

commonMistakes.why: Amico is masculine singular, so the fused form must be dell' (di + l'), not the feminine plural delle.

items.explanation: Each preposition follows the same pattern across il/lo/la/l'/i/gli/le.

summary: A, di, da, in and su fuse with the definite article whenever the noun needs one.
The pattern is regular across all five prepositions: al/allo/alla/all'/ai/agli/alle, and so on.
No article needed, no fusion — fixed expressions like a scuola, a casa stay unfused.
